'''Karen Keskulla Uhlenbeck''' [[ForMemRS]] (born August 24, 1942) is an American mathematician and one of the founders of modern [[geometric analysis]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.npr.org/2019/03/19/704841252/u-s-mathematician-becomes-first-woman-to-win-abel-prize-math-s-nobel | title=U.S. Mathematician Becomes First Woman To Win Abel Prize, 'Math's Nobel' | author=Bill Chappell | date=19 March 2019 | publisher=NPR | access-date=8 April 2019}}</ref> She is a professor emerita of mathematics at the [[University of Texas at Austin]], where she held the [[Sid W. Richardson Foundation]] Regents Chair.<ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor Biography|id=Uhlenbeck_Karen|mode=cs1}}</ref><ref name="asc">{{Cite journal |url=http://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/uhlenbk.htm |title=Karen Uhlenbeck |website=Biographies of Women Mathematicians |publisher=[[Agnes Scott College]]}}</ref><ref name="umich">{{Cite journal |url=http://www.ur.umich.edu/9900/Dec06_99/12.htm |title=Michigan Great Karen K. Uhlenbeck: Pioneer in mathematical analysis—and for women mathematicians |journal=The University Record |first=Lee |last=Katterman |date=December 6, 1999 |publisher=University of Michigan |access-date=December 19, 2014 |archive-date=June 11, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611021150/http://ur.umich.edu/9900/Dec06_99/12.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> She is currently a distinguished visiting professor at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/karen-uhlenbeck|title=Karen Uhlenbeck|website=Institute for Advanced Study|language=en|access-date=2019-08-07}}</ref> and a visiting senior research scholar at [[Princeton University]].<ref name="CBS" />

Uhlenbeck was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 2007.<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Karen+K.+Uhlenbeck&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-05-17|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> She won the 2019 [[Abel Prize]] for "her pioneering achievements in geometric [[partial differential equations]], [[gauge theory]], and [[integrable system]]s, and for the fundamental impact of her work on [[mathematical analysis|analysis]], [[geometry]] and [[mathematical physics]]."<ref name="citation">{{cite web |title=2019: Karen Keskulla Uhlenbeck |url=https://abelprize.no/abel-prize-laureates/2019 |access-date=22 July 2022 |publisher=The Abel Prize}}</ref> She is the first, and so far only, woman to win the prize since its inception in 2003.<ref>{{cite magazine| url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/karen-uhlenbeck-first-woman-win-maths-top-prize-180971758/ | title=Karen Uhlenbeck Is the First Woman to Win Math's Top Prize | author=Meilan Solly | date=20 March 2019 | magazine=Smithsonian Magazine| access-date=8 April 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Chang |first=Kenneth |title=Karen Uhlenbeck Is First Woman to Receive Abel Prize in Mathematics – Dr. Uhlenbeck helped pioneer geometric analysis, developing techniques now commonly used by many mathematicians. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/03/19/science/karen-uhlenbeck-abel-prize.html |date=March 19, 2019 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=March 19, 2019}}</ref> She donated half of the prize money to organizations which promote more engagement of women and other minorities in research mathematics.

== Life and career ==
Uhlenbeck was born in [[Cleveland]], Ohio, to engineer Arnold Keskulla and schoolteacher and artist Carolyn Windeler Keskulla. While she was a child, the family moved to [[New Jersey]].<ref name="abel">{{cite web |url=https://www.abelprize.no/c73996/binfil/download.php?tid=74122 |title=A biography of Karen Keskulla Uhlenbeck |first=Jim |last=Al-Khalili |author-link=Jim Al-Khalili |website=abelprize.no |access-date=15 July 2019 |archive-date=July 15, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190715165708/https://www.abelprize.no/c73996/binfil/download.php%3Ftid%3D74122 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Uhlenbeck's maiden name, Keskulla, comes from ''Keskküla'' and from her grandfather who was Estonian, while her current surname is Dutch.<ref name="celebratio">{{cite web|title=Interview with Karen Uhlenbeck    |author= Allyn Jackson    |year= 2018 |url=http://celebratio.org/Uhlenbeck_K/article/634/ |work=Celebratio Mathematica }}</ref> Uhlenbeck received her [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] (1964) from the [[University of Michigan]].<ref name="mactutor" /><ref name="umich" /> She began her graduate studies at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]] at [[New York University]], and married biophysicist [[Olke C. Uhlenbeck]] (the son of physicist [[George Uhlenbeck]]) in 1965. When her husband went to Harvard, she moved with him and restarted her studies at [[Brandeis University]], where she earned an [[Master of Arts|MA]] (1966) and PhD (1968) under the supervision of [[Richard Palais]].<ref name="mactutor" /><ref name="umich" /> Her doctoral dissertation was titled ''The Calculus of Variations and Global Analysis''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy |id=4834}}</ref>

After temporary jobs at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and [[University of California, Berkeley]], and having difficulty finding a permanent position with her husband because of the "anti-nepotism" rules then in place that prevented hiring both a husband and wife even in distinct departments of a university, she took a faculty position at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] in 1971.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cooke |first1=Roger |title=The History of Mathematics: A Brief Course |url=https://archive.org/details/historymathemati00cook |url-access=limited |date=2005 |publisher=Wiley-Interscience |location=Hoboken, NJ |isbn=978-0-471-44459-6 |page=[https://archive.org/details/historymathemati00cook/page/n94 76] |edition=2.}}</ref> However, she disliked Urbana and moved to the [[University of Illinois at Chicago]] in 1976 as well as separating from her first husband Olke Uhlenbeck in the same year.<ref name="celebratio"/> From 1979 to 1981 Uhlenbeck served on the Council of the [[American Mathematical Society|AMS]] as a Member at Large.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AMS Committees |url=http://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/committees/mal-past.html |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=American Mathematical Society |language=en}}</ref> She moved again to the [[University of Chicago]] in 1983.<ref name="celebratio"/> In 1988, by which time she had married mathematician Robert F. Williams,<ref name="celebratio"/> she moved to the [[University of Texas at Austin]] as the Sid W. Richardson Foundation Regents Chairholder.<ref name="mactutor" /><ref name="asc" /><ref name="umich" /> Uhlenbeck is currently a professor emerita at the University of Texas at Austin,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ma.utexas.edu/component/cobalt/category-items/1-directory/15-mathematics?Itemid=1265|title=Mathematics Emeritus Faculty|publisher=University of Texas at Austin|access-date=March 16, 2024}}</ref> a visiting associate at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] and a visiting senior research scholar at [[Princeton University]].<ref name="CBS">{{cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/abel-prize-karen-uhlenbeck-a-woman-just-won-maths-nobel-prize-for-the-first-time-ever/|title=A woman just won the prize known as "math's Nobel" — for the first time ever|publisher=CBS News|last=Garrand|first=Danielle|date=March 19, 2019|access-date=March 19, 2019}}</ref>

== Research ==
Uhlenbeck is one of the founders of the field of [[geometric analysis]], a discipline that uses [[differential geometry]] to study the solutions to [[differential equation]]s and vice versa.<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=[[Quanta Magazine|Quanta]] |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/karen-uhlenbeck-uniter-of-geometry-and-analysis-wins-abel-prize-20190319/ |title=Karen Uhlenbeck, Uniter of Geometry and Analysis, Wins Abel Prize |first=Erica |last=Klarreich |author-link=Erica Klarreich |date=March 19, 2019}}</ref> She has also contributed to [[topological quantum field theory]] and [[integrable system]]s.<ref name="mactutor" /><ref name="noether">{{Cite journal |url=http://www.awm-math.org/noetherbrochure/Uhlenbeck88.html |title=Karen Uhlenbeck |website=Profiles of Women in Mathematics: The Emmy Noether Lectures |publisher=[[Association for Women in Mathematics]] |access-date=December 19, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150112115305/http://www.awm-math.org/noetherbrochure/Uhlenbeck88.html |archive-date=January 12, 2015 |url-status=dead }}.</ref>

Together with Jonathan Sacks in the early 1980s, Uhlenbeck established regularity estimates that have found applications to studies of the [[Singularity (mathematics)|singularities]] of [[harmonic map]]s and the existence of smooth local solutions to the [[Yang–Mills–Higgs equations]] in [[gauge theory (mathematics)|gauge theory]].{{ran|EMI}}{{ran|MIC}}{{ran|RSY}} In particular, [[Simon Donaldson]] describes their joint 1981 paper ''The existence of minimal immersions of 2-spheres''{{ran|EMI}} as a "landmark paper... which showed that, with a deeper analysis, [[calculus of variations|variational arguments]] can still be used to give general existence results" for harmonic map equations.<ref name=notices-2019/>
Building on these ideas, Uhlenbeck initiated a systematic study of the [[moduli space|moduli theory]] of [[minimal surfaces]] in hyperbolic [[3-manifold]]s (also called minimal submanifold theory) in her 1983 paper, ''Closed minimal surfaces in hyperbolic 3-manifolds''.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Closed Minimal Surfaces in Cusped Hyperbolic three-manifolds |url= https://www.math.csi.cuny.edu/~huang/cusp-arx.pdf |last1=Huang |first1=Zheng |last2=Wang |first2=Biao |journal=Geometriae Dedicata |volume=189 |issue=1 |year=2017 |pages=37–57 |doi= 10.1007/s10711-016-0215-8 |arxiv= 1507.04818 |s2cid= 67774341 }}</ref>{{ran|CMS}}

In particular, her work is described by [[Simon Donaldson]] in a survey of Yang–Mills geometry as foundational in the analytic aspects of the calculus of variations associated with the [[Yang–Mills equations|Yang–Mills functional]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Yang–Mills theory and Geometry |last=Donaldson |first=Simon K. |year=2005 |url=http://wwwf.imperial.ac.uk/~skdona/YMILLS.PDF}}</ref> A wider survey of her contributions to the field of calculus of variations was published by Simon Donaldson in the March 2019 issue of ''[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]''; Donaldson describes the work of Uhlenbeck, along with [[Shing-Tung Yau]], [[Richard Schoen]] and several others, as developing a... {{blockquote|...whole circle of ideas and techniques involving the dimension of singular sets, [[monotone function|monotonicity]], 'small energy' results, [[tangent cone]]s, etc. [that] has had a wide-ranging impact in many branches of differential geometry over the past few decades and forms the focus of much current research activity.<ref name=notices-2019>{{cite journal |title=Karen Uhlenbeck and the Calculus of Variations|first=Simon |last=Donaldson |author-link=Simon Donaldson|journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=66 |issue=3 |year=2019 |pages=303–313|doi= 10.1090/noti1806 |doi-access=free }}</ref>}}

== Outreach ==
In 1991, Uhlenbeck co-founded, with [[Herbert Clemens]] and [[Dan Freed]], the Park City Mathematics Institute (PCMI) with the mission to "provide an immersive educational and professional development opportunity for several parallel communities from across the larger umbrella of the mathematics profession."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/pcmi/about|title=About PCMI: Mission, History, Summer Session|date=January 27, 2018|publisher=Institute for Advanced Study|access-date=March 19, 2019}}</ref><ref name="CBS" /> Uhlenbeck also co-founded the Women and Mathematics Program at the Institute for Advanced Study "with the mission to recruit and retain more women in mathematics."<ref>{{cite web|title=Women and Mathematics|date=August 5, 2008|url=https://www.math.ias.edu/wam|publisher=Institute for Advanced Study|access-date=March 19, 2019}}</ref><ref name="CBS" /> British theoretical physicist and author [[Jim Al-Khalili]] describes Uhlenbeck as a "role model" for her work in promoting a career in mathematics to young people, particularly women.<ref name="BBC_Abel" />

== Personal life ==
Uhlenbeck is a self-described "messy reader" and "messy thinker", with boxes of books stacked on her desk at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study. In spontaneous remarks made to Institute colleagues after winning the Abel Prize in March 2019, Uhlenbeck noted that for lack of prominent female role models during her apprenticeship in the field of mathematics, she had instead emulated chef [[Julia Child]]: "She knew how to pick the turkey up off the floor and serve it".<ref name=Roberts8April>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/08/science/uhlenbeck-bubbles-math-physics.html |title=In Bubbles, She Sees a Mathematical Universe |first=Siobhan|last=Roberts|date=8 April 2019|access-date=9 April 2019|work=The New York Times}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
In March 2019, Uhlenbeck became the first woman to receive the [[Abel Prize]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ndtv.com/world-news/us-mathematician-karen-uhlenbeck-becomes-first-woman-to-win-prestigious-abel-prize-2010155|title=US Mathematician Becomes First Woman To Win Prestigious Abel Prize|website=NDTV.com|access-date=2019-03-20}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2019-03-19 |title=Bubble maths researcher wins top award |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-47613929 |access-date=2026-06-29 |work=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref> with the award committee citing the decision for "her pioneering achievements in geometric [[partial differential equations]], [[gauge theory]] and [[integrable system]]s, and for the fundamental impact of her work on [[mathematical analysis|analysis]], [[geometry]] and [[mathematical physics]]."<ref name="citation" /> [[Hans Munthe-Kaas]], who chaired the award committee, stated that "Her theories have revolutionised our understanding of minimal surfaces, such as more general minimisation problems in higher dimensions".<ref name="BBC_Abel">{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-47613929 |title=Bubble maths researcher wins top award |author=Pallab Ghosh |publisher=BBC |date=March 19, 2019 |access-date=March 19, 2019}}</ref> She donated half of the cash prize to two organizations, the EDGE Foundation (which subsequently set up the [[EDGE Foundation#The Karen EDGE Fellowship Program|Karen EDGE Fellowship Program]]), and the Institute for Advanced Study's Women and Mathematics (WAM) Program.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202002/rnoti-p228.pdf Gift from Uhlenbeck Funds Karen EDGE Fellowship] Notices of the AMS, Vol 67, No 2, pp 228–230</ref>

Uhlenbeck also won the [[National Medal of Science]] in 2000,<ref name="mactutor" /><ref name="asc" /><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=366 |title=The President's National Medal of Science: Recipient Details |access-date=December 13, 2009 |publisher=[[National Science Foundation]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.utexas.edu/news/2000/11/13/nr_science/ |title=UT Austin mathematics professor wins National Medal of Science |publisher=Univ. of Texas |date=November 13, 2000 |access-date=December 19, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121105204337/http://www.utexas.edu/news/2000/11/13/nr_science/ |archive-date=November 5, 2012 |url-status=dead }}.</ref> and the [[Leroy P. Steele Prize]] for Seminal Contribution to Research of the [[American Mathematical Society]] in 2007, "for her foundational contributions in analytic aspects of mathematical gauge theory",<ref name="mactutor" /><ref name="asc" /> based on her 1982 papers "Removable singularities in Yang–Mills fields"{{ran|RSY}} and "Connections with bounds on curvature".{{ran|CLP}} She became a [[MacArthur Fellow]] in 1983<ref name="mactutor" /><ref name="asc" /> and a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1985.<ref name="mactutor" /><ref name="asc" /> She was elected as a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1986.<ref name="mactutor" /><ref name="asc" /><ref name="umich" /> She became a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]] in 2001,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.utexas.edu/news/2001/04/23/nr_guggenheim/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20141220044434/http://www.utexas.edu/news/2001/04/23/nr_guggenheim/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 20, 2014 |title=Three UT Austin professors win prestigious Guggenheim Fellowships |publisher=Univ. of Texas |date=April 23, 2001 |access-date=December 19, 2014 }}.</ref>
an honorary member of the [[London Mathematical Society]] in 2008,<ref name="mactutor" /> and a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]] in 2012.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list |title=List of Fellows |publisher=American Mathematical Society |access-date=August 28, 2013}}.</ref>

The [[Association for Women in Mathematics]] included her in the 2020 class of AWM Fellows for "her groundbreaking and profound contributions to modern geometric analysis; for establishing a career as one of the greatest mathematicians of our time, despite the considerable challenges facing women when she entered the field; for using her experiences navigating these challenges to create and sustain programs to address them for future generations of women. For a lifetime of breaking barriers; and for being the first woman to win the Abel Prize".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://awm-math.org/awards/awm-fellows/2020-awm-fellows/|title=2020 Class of AWM Fellows|publisher=[[Association for Women in Mathematics]]|access-date=2019-11-08}}</ref>

She was the [[Noether Lecture]]r of the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]] in 1988.<ref name="noether" /> In 1990, she was a plenary speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]], as only the second woman (after [[Emmy Noether]]) to give such a lecture.<ref name="mactutor" /><ref name="asc" />

Her other awards include the University of Michigan alumna of the year (1984),<ref name="umich" /> the [[Sigma Xi]] Common Wealth Award for Science and Technology (1995),<ref name="umich" /> and honorary doctorates from the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] (2000),<ref name="mactutor" /> [[Ohio State University]] (2001),<ref name="mactutor" /><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.osu.edu/universityawards/dsa/honorary.html |title=Honorary Degree – University Awards & Recognition – The Ohio State University |website=osu.edu|access-date=March 19, 2019}}</ref> [[University of Michigan]] (2004),<ref name="mactutor" /> [[Harvard University]] (2007),<ref name="mactutor" /> and [[Princeton University]] (2012).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2012/06/05/princeton-awards-six-honorary-degrees |title=Princeton awards six honorary degrees |website=Princeton University |language=en|access-date=March 8, 2019}}</ref>
